And when we release this concept that we've got, it's not actually legislation yet, but when we release the concept so that people could look at it and weigh it, the response we got was about what we expected. There were a lot of people that said, interesting. This is a serious proposal. Maybe we got a ought to take it into consideration and talk to the stakeholders and so forth. There were those people who said, hell no. And they've always said that about dam removal. And that was kind of their first reaction. But I think when we get an opportunity to talk to the different stakeholders and see what's in that for them and get them looking past what currently exists and what we want to exist in the future that will bring many of them around, but certainly the Pacific Northwest delegation, both Democrats and Republicans need to be a part of this.
We have a Democrat in the White House. Democrats are controlling the House and the Senate with Vice President Harris now being the tiebreaker.
Right.
Would you have introduced this idea if former President Trump had won re-election or if Congress wasn't controlled by Democrats right now?

Yeah, we would have. Like I said, we've been working on this for three years and We decided to go with it regardless of how the election turns out. We have been in contact with our senators to brief them on what is being proposed. And we have been in contact with Senator Wyden, who now chairs the Senate Finance Committee, where much of the financing for this would have to come from. So we've been in contact with a lot of legislators on this proposal, and we've gotten Kind of that reaction I was telling you about it.
People kind of saying,
okay, let's kind of sit back and see how the public reacts to this before we jump on board or or so forth. And that's kind of what we expected.

So, you know, we chatted about these Democratic senators in Oregon and Washington a minute ago, Congressman, and they have not all been supportive of removing the dams in the past. I mean, in fact, let's talk about Senator Cantwell, in particular. Are you trying to force her hand on this environmental issue, or are you hoping that maybe with time she will come around, as you say?

Well, I'm hopeful that all of the senators, not just the Democratic ones in Washington and Oregon, but the Republicans in Idaho and Montana will look at this not just as a proposal to remove dams. It's much broader than that. The stakeholders that we have identified that need assistance in transforming the way they do things, actually come out ahead in this. And if people will sit back and look at the entire thing, the entire proposal, rather than just saying remove dams, don't remove dams. of these 25 or so collaborative organizations that we've had over the years that have looked at different ways to save salmon. They get together and they talk and they go, oh, yeah, we can prove the habitat here and we could do this and maybe the fish passage here. They all make these all these agreements, but then when it comes down to the real issue, which is removal of dams, they just break apart. And
so

people need to view this as more than just removing the dams. It is also helping the communities. It is truly helping agriculture and agriculture in the second district really would benefit from this. And it's helping those communities transform their economies, those that would be affected most, like Lewiston, Carxton, Tri-Cities, and so forth.

So here in Idaho, Congressman Russ Folcher has made some public statements since the news of your proposal broke. Does that sound like he's really in favor of it? But how important is his support, but also the support of Senator's Russian Crapo?

Well, I think their support is important. We'd certainly like to have them on board, but I understand where they're coming from. They're being very cautious about the issue. We've been talking about taking dams out, or at least people have been talking about it for 25 or 30 years. And in fact, I was very opposed to the very first time I heard it. I thought that was kind of a crazy idea. And I said at the time that we need to try everything else before we went to the extreme of removing dams. But the reality is we have now tried everything else. And we don't have that much longer to save these salmon, or they're going to be extinct. And once they've gone extinct, you don't get them back. So I think they're being very cautious. And I think they want to hear from the stakeholders about what their thoughts are on this and if there are other challenges that we haven't anticipated and things that we need to look at, that's why we put out this concept so that we can hear from people from all sides of the issue and then and hear from them before we start drafting legislation.

turn_text: Your idea is to have this $34 billion proposal tied to President Biden's upcoming infrastructure bill. And this bill is very important to his agenda. So have you been in touch with the White House about this? And if you have, what kind of interest have they indicated?

I have not personally been in contact with him. We haven't got that far yet in determining what their agenda is going to be beyond the COVID release that they're working on now. But there have been senators that have talked to the administration and there seems to be some interest there.

And what about response? I mean, here we've talked about all the politicians. What about response from the public? I mean, in particular, you know, people who live in these towns that will be the most impacted by this.

Well, you know, it's, it's been across the board. As I said earlier, the from the people that looked at it and said, okay, they want to remove the dams, hell no, they're opposed to it. They haven't sometimes seen the entire proposal or considered the entire proposal. all the way to those who think, man, we've been wanting to do this for 25 years. Now we finally got somebody that's willing to do it. And so the public opinion spreads completely across the board. And what we've got to do is try to consolidate that with educating people about what this proposal actually is. As I said, it's much broader than just dam removal.
So what are the next steps? I mean, have you started to draft legislation?

We have it yet. We want to hear from our constituents first and the different industries and user groups and hear what they have to say, take into consideration their thoughts and concerns before we start drafting legislation. And I would expect over the next month or so we'll probably start drafting legislation.

Well, and this isn't the first time, Congressman, that you have taken up an issue with some complicated stakeholder interest. I'm curious about how different from previous work on issues, this is in particular when you were trying to protect the Boulder White Clouds.

Well, Boulder White Clouds took us a number of years to do, and we learned a lot from it on how to bring people together in the primary goal or thing that you need to do in bringing people together is listen to them and take into consideration their concerns and so forth. And so we'll be doing a lot of that and have been doing for the last three years before we dropped this proposal. But we'll be doing a lot more of that. But this is, and some people have called it the biggest environmental restoration program in the world. So it is very complicated and has many, many different facets of it that make it really, really complicated, but that's why it's so comprehensive.
I really want to thank you for your time to talk to us about this because it is a complicated issue and so many sides to it, so many stakeholders, as you said. So appreciate your time.
Thank you very much. Appreciate it, Emma.

Well, we've been talking with Congressman Mike Simpson about his new proposal to recover the salmon. We will link his idea on our website so all of you can take a look at it. Again, Congressman, thanks for your time.
